1. Who Ale Is

Ale (Alejandra Hernández) is a queer Mexican-American poet and memory worker from San Diego, California. She holds an MFA from San Diego State University. She is the sole creator, editor, and maintainer of Hot Wheels & High Heels.

What she’s said about herself:

  • “I’m a queer Mexican-American poet and memory worker from San Diego”
  • “I am interested in memory work and interviewing memory workers”
  • “Woman first, mother second has been the driving force behind many of my decisions”
  • “My cousins are my best friends. Nothing matters without them. Without them there is no love, no poetry.”
  • “I’m from San Diego and have no aspirations to leave; San Diego is too beautiful”
  • “I am not amateur”
  • “I’m smart af”
  • “My sibling said it’s very myspace and my heart was happy”
  • “I’m a millennial, myspace was my first site. But it’s 2026 now and I’m a grown up and a literari professional”
  • “The boring ass jargon every other literary publication uses — they all sound the same and have no vibe. we stick to our vibe. millennials all the way bro. cars cars cars go vroooooooom”
  • “I got told to grow up and be professional one too many times in grad school and its affecting my swag”
  • “I was trying to stay away from bias language and generalizations”
  • “We gotta keep our language fresh fam. Remember more intimate, inviting someone into the bedroom. Less stale ass academic sentences”
  • “I like rearranging my room a lot”
  • “My constant editing is because I like rearranging my room a lot lol”

Core identity markers:

  • Memory worker, not archivist
  • Anti-jargon, pro-intimacy
  • MySpace energy meets scholarly rigor
  • Collecting, not teaching
  • The project is personal — 8 years of thinking, reading, writing, and crying because no one understood her vision

2. The Project Vision

Hot Wheels & High Heels is a living millennial memory project disguised as a literary publication. It is not a magazine that happens to have a research section. It is a memory work project that uses literary publication as its method.

What Ale has said about the project:

  • “humans are beautiful and creative and look what we made. millennials, the web, the future. it’s all connected. it’s beautiful.”
  • “the site is perfect as is, we are just building towards that dissertation now”
  • “I’m showcasing data and findings in the hopes that someone will contribute their experiences / memories / creative content to this archive”
  • “The point isn’t really to teach, it’s to collect”
  • “Millennials don’t need anyone else telling us what our life was. We know what it was. Let us tell you what it was.”
  • “This is 8 years worth of thinking, reading and writing, and crying because no one understood my vision. Let’s not fuck it up.”

The Origin: The project began as a poetry manuscript — love poems to a generation. Ale was originally writing love poems to singing voices and dancing bodies. As the poems accumulated, she realized they were no longer about singing and dancing. They were love poems to a generation. The phrase “epoch-making,” used to describe The Canterbury Tales, sparked the framework: “It’s easy to forget how epoch-making it is. It tells us, as nothing else does, how the different levels of medieval society dressed, talked, joked, swore and viewed one another.” Ale uses 21st century vernacular purposefully in her poetry because of the intricate ways love shows up in today’s world. “It is also easy to forget that I am a 21st century poet. I am part of a generation that was named after the turn of the millennium.”

The manuscript became a research project. The research project became an archive. The archive became a website.

The Central Question: What happens when personal memory, cultural history, and digital platforms become the same thing? This is not a thesis to prove — it is a question to explore through collection.

The Double Perspective: Ale’s original framework. Experience Self + Narrator Self = Double Perspective. Every component of the experience self has a partner in the narrator self. Neither controls the other. They are interdependent. The Drivers (interviews) are the experience self — living it, reacting, no hindsight. The Trunk (research) is the narrator self — organizing, interpreting, creating meaning from distance. The timeline is the distance between them. This framework was built from Vivian Gornick’s “The Situation and the Story” and Phillip Lopate’s “To Show and To Tell.”

The Epoch: The Millennial Epoch is not synonymous with the millennial age cohort. It is a series of sociopolitical and socioeconomic events that dramatically affected the development of the millennial age cohort and those following. “The epoch made the millennials, not the other way around.” People who came of age prior to the start of this epoch do not fit — their development wasn’t affected by the same events. Ale is the editor. She decides who fits the vibe. The epoch boundaries are: the timeline begins in 1981/1982 with the first millennials born and Reagan’s inauguration, and continues to the present.

The Methodology:

  • Collecting, not teaching
  • The archive is participatory — submission form, surveys, invitations to contribute
  • “My analysis will come later once I have compiled enough research and reference material”
  • The Trunk is the research. The Drivers are the witnesses. The Social Archive is the evidence.
  • Context matters more than nostalgia

The Audience (in priority order):

  1. Future Contributors / Researchers interested in Memory Work
  2. Literary Magazine Editors / Poets and MFA students
  3. Californian creatives, but more importantly Millennial creatives
  4. Friends and Family / General Readers

The User Journey: “Off site → contributors page or trunk → explore site → subscribe or share content” “Sharing content like in a chain-mail type of way. Please read this and share it with three people who will share it with three people”

The Vibe: A serious intellectual project with the energy of a 2007 MySpace page built by someone who became a scholar. Intimacy is the counterforce to professionalism. Intimacy is methodology — the site should feel like inviting someone into your bedroom. The automotive metaphor (Drivers, Trunk, Revving Up) is structural architecture, not decoration.

3. Foundational Documents

These documents exist outside the website. They are Ale’s academic work, research notes, and creative writing. They inform everything on the site. Nothing from these documents is pasted directly onto the website — the creative work is intended for publication.

3.1 The Manuscript: Love Poems to a Generation

Ale’s MFA thesis / poetry manuscript. Originally conceived as love poems to singing voices and dancing bodies, it became love poems to a generation. Key concerns: public vs. private settings for love in the 21st century, social media as a space where relationships form and end, dating apps as separate from social media, the expectation of a digital footprint documenting love, the pressure to perform relationships online, the question of why poets would avoid including social media as a space where love manifests. This is the creative origin of the entire project. Not on the website.

3.2 An Impossible Archaeology of Nostalgia

Ale’s academic paper. Seven sections that bridge personal narrative and archival theory:

  1. Memory — personal recollection, unaided, what you remember without looking anything up
  2. Aided Memory — fact-checked, timeline-based, what the archive confirms. Includes the color-coded timeline system (blue for commencement, green for acquisitions, gray for closures, red for political, orange for user references, purple for feature changes)
  3. Distorted Memory — collective vs. individual memory. The Dress at the family party. The Berlin Wall vs. social media moments. How the archive codetermines memory
  4. Familial Memory — email threads, Google Groups, Ale’s tia printing out the emails, “Who keeps the archive?”
  5. Questioning the Archive — surveillance, digital sobriety, “You will never find me. You will always find me.”
  6. Futuristic Memory — the double perspective as a tool for memory work, not just creative writing
  7. The Documentary — internet comments as evidence, “you are the documentary,” users as memory workers creating their own archive

Key sources: Derrida (Archive Fever), Berners-Lee (Information Management: A Proposal), Manoff (Theories of the Archive from Across the Disciplines). The personal narrative voice in this paper is the closest to Ale’s creative voice.

3.3 Research Outline & Annotated Bibliography

Working document with key quotes and annotations from Ale’s readings. Researchers and concepts that appear on the site:

  • Derrida: arkheion (residence of the archons, place of authority), archons (guardians with power to interpret archives), arca (the chest, the Ark of the Covenant), death drive (violence of forgetting), pleasure principle (external place of consignation promising repetition), technology as prosthesis (archive structure codetermines memory), the future orientation of the archive (integrity, openness, hope), repression vs. suppression. Archive Fever (1995). → Appears in: Field Notes accordion, Blessings page epigraph, Connections map
  • Berners-Lee: hypertext, hypermedia, universal readership, universal authorship, future-proofing, information loss as motivating problem, the web as unfinished system. “Information Management: A Proposal” (1989/1990). → Appears in: Field Notes accordion, Connections map
  • Manoff: archives and democracy, no political power without control of the archive, archives are not neutral, politics of preservation and deletion, electronic archives have different implications than paper. “Theories of the Archive from Across the Disciplines” (2004). → Appears in: Field Notes accordion, Connections map
  • Tošić: parallel truths (subjective archiving can lead to objective research results), digital mini-archives (social media users as curators and interpreters of history), utopian potential, transformability, fragility of digital archives. “Digital Mini-Archives” (2024). → Appears in: Field Notes accordion, Social Archive definition, Connections map
  • Ismail: memes as archival discourse, virality/mutability/intertextuality as three qualities of born-digital archival value, emotional presence, platform-centered stewardship, community-driven archives. “Born-Digital Memes as Archival Discourse” (2025). → Appears in: Field Notes accordion, Going Viral section description, Connections map
  • Vlassenroot: web archiving and social media, social media content as born-digital heritage, network-informed economy, public vs. private sphere. “Web-archiving and social media” (2021). → Appears in: Field Notes accordion
  • Roulston & deMarrais: traditional archive characteristics (static, unique, authentic), archival value requires structure and context. “Exploring the Archives” (2021). → Appears in: Field Notes accordion
  • Gebeil & Peyssard: web archives as digital heritage, digital sobriety, linked data and AI. “Exploring the Archived Web” (2024). → Appears in: Field Notes accordion
  • Gornick: The Situation and the Story. The situation is the context; the story is the insight one has come to say. Without detachment there can be no story. Memory as organizing principle. → Appears in: Field Notes accordion, Double Perspective table
  • Lopate: To Show and To Tell. Turning oneself into a character is release from narcissism. Facts delimit; truths are what we make of them. The narrator can peek ahead. Suspense in reflection. → Appears in: Field Notes accordion, Double Perspective framework

3.4 The Double Perspective Framework & Presentation Notes

Ale’s original framework. The formula: Experience Self + Narrator Self = Double Perspective. The full table:

Experience Self + Narrator Self = Result
Past + Present = Time
Reactive + Organized = Structure
Blind spots + Self-awareness = Insight
Objectivity + Subjectivity = Interpretation
Veracity / literal truth + Authenticity / literary truth = The story
Show + Tell = Narrative
Situation / context + Story / insight = Meaning
Experience Self + Narrator Self = Double Perspective

Key principles: The character lives in the past; the narrator lives in the present. The character reacts; the narrator organizes. Objectivity belongs to the experience self (relaying facts as you experienced them); subjectivity belongs to the narrator (interpreting through a lens). “Authenticity is the magic that happens in the personal narrative.” Neither self controls the other. They are interdependent. If there is no distance between the experience and the writing, the double perspective is hard to pull off. This framework underlies the entire site architecture: Drivers = experience self, Trunk = narrator self, timeline = the distance.

3.5 The Word Bank

The original seed that became the timeline and connections map. A list of epoch-defining terms: Post-Late-Capitalism, Ronald Reagan, War on Drugs, Maturity Ratings, Columbine, y2k, 9/11, Hurricane Katrina, 2008 Market Crash, Gig Economy, Data Colonialism, Resilience Narrative, White Supremacy, Police Brutality, MAGA, Covid-19, Artificial Intelligence. Originally displayed as a grid using the “ugh-list” CSS class. Some terms became timeline events. Some became concepts on the connections map. Some are still waiting to be developed.

4. Site Architecture

4.1 Technical Foundation

  • Platform: Jekyll static site generator
  • Hosting: GitHub Pages
  • Domain: hotwheelsandhighheels.com
  • CSS: Single file at /assets/css/styles.css (~2000+ lines, 26 organized sections)
  • JavaScript: Vanilla JS, no frameworks or libraries
  • Fonts: Google Fonts — Playfair Display, Cormorant Garamond, Lora
  • Plugins: jekyll-feed, jekyll-sitemap, jekyll-seo-tag
  • Permalink: pretty (clean URLs without .html)
  • Forms: Formspree for the submission form (/submit/)
  • Newsletter: Buttondown (free tier)
  • SEO: Google Search Console verified, sitemap submitted
  • .htaccess: Force HTTPS, force trailing slashes, remove old Squarespace rewrite rule

4.3 Layouts & Includes

default.html — Used by: Home, About, Trunk pages, 404, meAF, Blessings, Submit, all surveys. Includes: head.html, header.html, content area, footer.html. Has back-to-top button and theme toggle button. Contains toggleTheme() function, selectAllText() function (for survey copy-paste), openBlessingLightbox() and closeBlessingLightbox() functions. Body has NO special class.

post.html — Used by: Contributor pages, Drivers gallery, Revving Up. Includes: head.html, header.html, content area (NO footer). Has <body class="post"> for CSS scoping. Contains toggleTheme(), toggleInterests() (for MySpace ✦ dropdown), openLightbox() and closeLightbox() functions. Has back-to-top button and theme toggle button.

head.html — Meta charset, viewport, title. Theme flash prevention script (checks localStorage before page renders). Google Fonts preconnect. Stylesheet link. Favicon links (SVG + PNG + apple-touch-icon). SEO plugin tags (feed_meta, seo).

header.html — Navigation bar with logo (“Hot Wheels & High Heels” in Cormorant Garamond). Hamburger menu button with ARIA labels (aria-expanded, aria-controls). Menu items looped from _data/menu.yml. toggleMenu() function with ARIA state management.

footer.html — 4Runner image with onclick="revTheEngine()". Dedication text (“RIP My 2000 Toyota 4runner”). Preloaded Audio objects for instant playback on click. revTheEngine() function picks random sound, resets to beginning, plays, triggers shake animation (guarded by prefers-reduced-motion).

banner.html — Single <img class="banner"> tag included on home page. Detailed alt text describing the photo.

4.4 The Three Interlocking Systems

The site organizes information through three systems that talk to each other. Every artifact in the Social Archive is tagged with at least one from each system.

System 1: Timeline Categories (7) Used on: Epoch timeline page, Connections map, artifact tags

  • Technology (cyan) — tools that shaped the epoch
  • Politics (orchid) — laws, elections, conflicts, policies
  • Culture (mint) — shared symbols, stories, moments
  • Economics (silver) — crashes, debt, gig economy, precarity
  • Environment (coral) — climate, disasters, data centers, extinction
  • Local Memory (chartreuse) — neighborhoods, landmarks, communities at street level
  • Documentation (gold) — witnessing, recording, testimony, bystander footage

System 2: Quote Themes (7) Used on: Drivers quote page, tagged quotes on contributor pages, Connections map, artifact tags

  • Place (chartreuse) — locations where memory takes root
  • Loss (coral) — things that disappeared
  • Intimacy (gold) — friendship, family, vulnerability
  • Web (cyan) — experiences mediated by digital life
  • Identity (orchid) — race, gender, culture, faith
  • Creativity (mint) — art, poetry, music
  • Future (silver) — transition, technology, hope

System 3: Archive Sections (6) Used on: Social Archive page, Connections map, artifact tags

  • Upgrade You — technology changing how we communicate (5 artifacts)
  • Going Viral — memes, remixes, participatory culture (6 artifacts)
  • The Parasocial — celebrity/fan fourth-wall collapse (2 artifacts)
  • Broken Record — reboots, remakes, sequels (0 artifacts)
  • Between You & I — intimate moments meant for specific people (2 artifacts)
  • AI Reception — literary world responding to AI (42 artifacts)

How they connect: Each artifact’s data-tags attribute contains the archive section name + timeline categories + quote themes. The tagMap in the archive page JavaScript maps these to CSS classes for colored pills. The Connections map has nodes for all three systems with lines showing relationships.

The pairings across systems:

  • Place (quotes) ↔ Local Memory (timeline) — both chartreuse
  • Loss (quotes) ↔ Environment (timeline) — both coral
  • Intimacy (quotes) ↔ Documentation (timeline) — both gold
  • Web (quotes) ↔ Technology (timeline) — both cyan
  • Identity (quotes) ↔ Politics (timeline) — both orchid
  • Creativity (quotes) ↔ Culture (timeline) — both mint
  • Future (quotes) ↔ Economics (timeline) — both silver

The archive sections don’t have dedicated colors. In the tagMap, they map to the timeline category colors: Upgrade You→place (chartreuse), Going Viral→identity (orchid), The Parasocial→culture (mint), Broken Record→loss (coral), Between You & I→intimacy (gold).

4.5 The Color System

Seven Theme Colors:

Color Name CSS Variable Hex (Dark Mode) Hex (Light Mode)
Place (chartreuse) --theme-place #8fd3c7 #4f8f85
Loss (coral) --theme-loss #ff8c69 #d96b48
Intimacy (gold) --theme-intimacy #ffe066 #b8860b
Web (cyan) --theme-web #4df0ff #008fb3
Identity (orchid) --theme-identity #ffb3ff #9b5ca9
Creativity (mint) --theme-creativity #7fffd4 #2ca88f
Future (silver) --theme-future #e6e6e6 #666666

Site Identity Colors:

  • Pink: #ff00a3 (--pink) — sacred, used for H1, links, borders, Memory center node
  • Purple: #a300ff (--purple) — H2, H3, nav logo, secondary accents
  • Off-white: #f5f0f5 (--text) — body text on dark
  • Off-black: #0a0608 (--bg) — background on dark mode

Where colors are used:

  • Timeline legend buttons and pill tags use the seven theme colors
  • Quote blocks on the Drivers page use the seven theme colors for borders and text
  • Artifact metadata pills use timeline category colors
  • Connections map nodes use theme colors based on node type
  • Archive sections and site pages on the Connections map use silver (theme-future)

Pill tag opacities: Background at 0.12 opacity, border at 0.25 opacity. The .artifact-meta container has opacity: 1 to ensure pills render at full strength. All pill tags share a base style with border-radius: 12px, padding: 2px 8px, font-size: 7pt, letter-spacing: 0.12em, text-transform: uppercase.

About (/About/) — default layout. H1: “About” (centered, responsive). Drivers Gallery (/Drivers/) — post layout. Grid of contributor cards with cover images and name overlays. Feature card for Revving Up (placeholder until Carson goes live). Contributor Pages (/Drivers/Jon/, /Drivers/Alana/, etc.) — post layout. Standard template: cover photo banner (clickable lightbox), driver-name H1, bio card (photo + bio text + connect links with MySpace ✦ toggle and interests table), divider, poem section (optional, H1 creates anchor for poetry links), interview conversation (H3 questions, paragraph answers with tagged quotes linking to /Trunk/drivers/#[theme]), driver navigation (previous/next), lightbox div.

Trunk Dashboard (/Trunk/) — default layout. H1: “Trunk” (centered, responsive). Intro card: central question. 7 collection cards in 2-column grid: The Millennial Epoch, The Social Archive, The Drivers, Field Notes, Connections, Send Me Something, Blessings. Secret link to Memory Worker survey. Driver nav: Drivers ← → Home.

The Millennial Epoch (/Trunk/epoch/) — default layout. H1: “The Millennial Epoch.” Intro paragraph defining epoch vs. age cohort. Timeline legend with 7 filter buttons + Show All. 5 eras: Before the Web (1982–1994), Logging On (1995–2004), Always Online (2005–2010), Platform Life (2011–2020), After the Feed (2021–present). 80+ events, each with left/right alternating placement, category tags in data-category attribute, concept tags in data-concepts, pill tag spans. Filtering JavaScript hides/shows entries by category. Driver nav: Back to Trunk ← → View Artifacts.

The Social Archive (/Trunk/archive/) — default layout. H1: “The Social Archive.” Intro text about collecting epoch-forming content. 6 sections, each with description and artifact count. Each section contains an artifact slideshow with slides carrying data-title, data-origin, data-date, data-context, data-significance, and data-tags. Metadata context section updates on slide change. AI Reception uses separate slideshow system (42 randomly shuffled slides). Shared changeArtifactSlide() and updateArtifactMetadata() functions. Secret link to Camera Roll Dump survey. Driver nav: Explore Timeline ← → Flag down a Driver.

The Drivers (/Trunk/drivers/) — default layout. H1: “The Drivers.” Intro: “Seven themes, one pattern.” Theme legend with colored spans. Seven theme sections (Place, Loss, Web, Intimacy, Identity, Creativity, Future), each with 2-3 tagged quotes from contributors. Each quote is a blockquote with theme-specific border color, attribution link, and theme pill tags. HTML comments above each quote with contributor name, themes, and location. Driver nav: View Artifacts ← → Dig thru the glove box.

Field Notes (/Trunk/notes/) — default layout. H1: “Field Notes.” Three main sections: Foundations (What Is a Memory Worker?, What Is a Social Archive?, The Double Perspective with table, Born-Digital Heritage), The Internet as a Memory System (Why Social Media Is a Historical Record, The Problem of Digital Memory, The Death of Forgetting, The Internet Was Never Finished, The Web as an Archival Dream), Power & Ownership (Who Owns Memory?, Platform Death and Culture Loss, The Archive of Everyday Life). Open Questions section at the bottom. Reading Notes in accordions (Derrida, Berners-Lee, Manoff, Tošić, Ismail, Vlassenroot, Roulston & deMarrais, Gebeil & Peyssard, Gornick, Lopate). Bibliography link to Zotero. Driver nav: Flag down a driver ← → Check the road map.

Connections (/Trunk/connections/) — default layout. H1: “Connections.” Intro text about the visualization being a work in progress. Full-screen draggable map with SVG connection lines. ~75 nodes organized by type: Center (Memory, pink), Archive Sections (silver), Timeline Categories (theme-colored), Quote Themes (theme-colored), Key Concepts (various theme colors), Researchers (chartreuse), Contributors (orchid), Platforms (cyan), Site Pages (silver). Click-to-preview popup positioned near the clicked node with title, type, description, and optional “Visit page →” link. Drag-and-drop with hasMoved flag to prevent click-drag conflicts. previewData object with descriptions in Ale’s voice. Driver nav: Dig thru the glove box ← → Back to Trunk.

Revving Up (/revving-up/) — post layout. Teaser page with static-line animation, “Next Feature” label, “Revving Up” title, “something’s coming” subtitle. Buttondown subscribe form with “I saved you a seat!” label and “Save my seat” button. Will be taken offline when Carson goes live.

404 (/404/) — default layout. “Wrong Turn” H2, “Better luck next time foo!” text, secret link to 3AM survey, “Pop a U-turn” link to home. sitemap: false.

meAF (/meAF/) — default layout. Hidden page (sitemap: false). Raw, intimate about page. Blurbs section (“now” grid: reading, listening, watching, obsessed with, working on, thinking about). About me section (personal, voice-driven). Guestbook section with email prompt. Last updated date.

Blessings (/blessings/) — default layout. Hidden page (sitemap: false). Pull quote from Derrida’s Archive Fever: “And I have presented it to you as a memorial and as a reminder.” Blessing cards with image, name, project link, description, and personal note. Lightbox for images. Template comment for adding new entries. Ale is the first entry as an example.

Honeypot spam protection. Styled to match site design system.

Style Guide (/style-guide/) — default layout. Hidden page (sitemap: false). Reference for every component: typography, blockquote, image caption, tags, callout box, word bank, audio player, video embed, cover photo lightbox, divider, subscribe form, accordion.

Surveys (7 total) — All use default layout with sitemap: false. Each has survey-container div, H1 with ✦, description paragraph, divider, copy-area div with onclick="selectAllText(this)" containing the survey text in monospace, and “click, copy, paste” footer.

4.7 Design System

Non-Negotiables:

  • Pink #ff00a3 is sacred
  • The 4Runner footer stays
  • The custom double-heart cursor stays (disabled only for prefers-reduced-motion)
  • Dark mode is default; light mode is secondary
  • 600px single breakpoint — no intermediate breakpoints
  • 0.5px borders — intentionally hairline
  • Opacity-based hover states (0.7 → 1, or vice versa)
  • The automotive metaphor is architecture, not decoration
  • No new colors, fonts, or CSS frameworks without discussion
  • No AI-generated content on the site
  • Nothing from Ale’s creative writing documents goes on the site

Typography:

  • H1: Playfair Display italic, 400 weight, pink (--pink). 32pt default, larger on specific pages.
  • H2: Cormorant Garamond, 600 weight, purple (--purple). 24pt default.
  • H3: Lora, 500 weight, 12pt, 0.2em letter-spacing, uppercase, purple (--purple).
  • Body: Lora, 400 weight, 14pt, 1.75 line-height, off-white (--text).
  • Nav logo: Cormorant Garamond, 400 weight, 13pt, 0.22em letter-spacing, uppercase, purple.
  • Nav links: 11pt, 0.18em letter-spacing, uppercase.

Custom Cursor:

  • SVG double heart at /assets/svg/cursor.svg
  • Applied to body (auto), a and button (with hotspot coordinates 8 2)
  • Disabled by prefers-reduced-motion: reduce media query

Light/Dark Mode:

  • Dark mode is default (no data-theme attribute)
  • Light mode triggered by data-theme="light" on <html>
  • Theme preference saved to localStorage
  • Flash prevention: script in head.html checks localStorage before page render
  • Toggle button fixed bottom-left, ☼/☽ icon

Mobile (max-width: 600px):

  • Hamburger menu replaces nav links
  • Gallery grid: 2 columns
  • Trunk dashboard: single column
  • Timeline: single column, vertical line shifts left
  • Bio card: stacks vertically
  • Font sizes scale down
  • Connections map: min-height 400px, nodes truncated with ellipsis
  • Desktop nudge popup appears on mobile: “This project is best explored on desktop” with “got it ✦” dismiss button. Shows once per session.

Animations (guarded by prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference):

  • Static line flicker (teaser page)
  • 4Runner shake on click
  • Feature card pulse on hover

4.8 Key Components

  • Bio Card: Flexbox layout — profile image left (200px), bio text right. Stacks vertically on mobile. Connect links row with MySpace ✦ toggle.
  • Gallery Grid: CSS Grid, repeat(auto-fill, minmax(250px, 1fr)). Cards have 300px height, dark overlay with name on hover, brightness filter transition.
  • Lightbox: Fixed full-screen overlay, hidden by default, .open class toggles display. Pink close button. Functions in post.html layout (not duplicated on individual pages). Blessings page has its own lightbox functions in default.html.
  • Accordion: accordion-header button with accordion-icon (+/−), accordion-content div. toggleAccordion() function with ARIA state management.
  • Slideshow (AI Reception): .slideshow container, .slide divs with images and captions. Randomly shuffled on page load. changeSlide() function with prev/next. Separate system from artifact slideshows.
  • Artifact Slideshow: .artifact-slideshow container, .artifact-slide divs with data- attributes for metadata. changeArtifactSlide() and updateArtifactMetadata() functions shared across all archive sections. Counter display and prev/next buttons.
  • Pull Quote: Cormorant Garamond italic, 20pt, pink left border.
  • Tag: Inline pill, purple border, Lora font, 9pt, uppercase.
  • Callout Box: Pink left border, subtle background.
  • Timeline: Vertical pink line at 50%, year bubbles centered, event entries alternating left/right with category pill tags. Filtering JavaScript shows/hides by data-category.
  • Connections Map: Absolutely positioned draggable nodes, SVG connection lines. positionNodes(), drawLines(), drag-and-drop with hasMoved flag, preview popup on click.
  • MySpace Interests: Hidden table behind ✦ toggle. toggleInterests() function. myspace-interests div with interests-table.
  • Secret ✦ Links: .secret-link class. Pink, 0.3 opacity, 1.0 on hover, custom cursor, no underline. Used for survey links and easter eggs.
  • Surveys: survey-container with copy-area div. selectAllText() function on click for easy copy-paste.
  • Submission Form: Styled form fields matching site design. Pink focus borders, custom radio buttons, file upload, category dropdown.
  • Buttondown Form: Single-line flex layout, pink-bordered email input and submit button.
  • Double Perspective Table: Collapsed borders, pink plus signs, purple result column, italic last row.
  • Driver Navigation: Flexbox row with previous/next links, pink top border separator.

4.9 CSS Architecture

styles.css is organized into 26 numbered sections:

  1. Fonts & Variables — Google Fonts import, CSS custom properties, light mode overrides
  2. Accessibility Foundation — reduced motion, skip link, focus-visible, sr-only
  3. Global Elements — body, headings, paragraphs, links, lists, editor-name, ride-link, about-page, trunk-page
  4. Navigation — nav bar, logo, menu, hamburger toggle
  5. Banner & Footer — banner glow, footer image, dedication text
  6. Buttons & Interactive — back-to-top, theme toggle, custom cursor
  7. Contributor Pages — bio card, gallery, lightbox, cover photo link, driver nav
  8. Components — pull quote, caption, tag, callout, audio player, video embed, accordion, slideshow, double perspective table
  9. Email Signup Form — Buttondown form styling
  10. Teaser Page — static lines, content, subscribe section
  11. Color-Coded Quote System — tag colors, quote blocks, attribution, legend, witness pill tags
  12. Wiki Page (Legacy) — old wiki styles
  13. Trunk Dashboard — grid, cards, hover effects
  14. Archive Artifact System — artifact layout, context, description, significance, metadata, artifact slideshow
  15. Connections Map — container, SVG lines, nodes, theme colors, center node, preview popup
  16. Epoch Timeline — legend, era headers, vertical line, year bubbles, entries, category pill tags
  17. Keyframes — flicker, pulse, carShake
  18. Mobile Styles — all responsive overrides at 600px breakpoint
  19. Animations (Motion-Safe) — wrapped in prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference
  20. meAF Page — container, header, sections, now grid, guestbook
  21. MySpace Interests — connect links, separators, toggle, table
  22. MySpace Surveys — survey container, copy area
  23. Secret ✦ Links — opacity, hover, cursor
  24. Submission Form — form layout, inputs, selects, fieldset, radio buttons, submit button
  25. Mobile Desktop Nudge — popup positioning, text, button
  26. Blessings Page — card layout, image, text, project link, note

4.10 JavaScript Overview

In default.html:

  • toggleTheme() — flips between dark (default) and light mode, updates localStorage and button icon
  • Theme icon update on page load (checks localStorage)
  • selectAllText(element) — selects all text in a survey copy-area for easy copy-paste
  • openBlessingLightbox(src) / closeBlessingLightbox() — lightbox for Blessings page images
  • Back-to-top button: window.scrollTo({top:0, behavior: 'smooth'})

In post.html:

  • toggleTheme() — same as default.html
  • Theme icon update on page load
  • toggleInterests(el) — toggles .open class on MySpace interests table
  • openLightbox() / closeLightbox() — lightbox for contributor cover photos

In footer.html:

  • Audio objects preloaded with preload = 'auto' and audio.load() to eliminate mobile lag
  • revTheEngine() — plays random 4Runner sound, triggers shake animation (motion-safe only)

In header.html:

  • toggleMenu() — toggles nav menu and hamburger button, updates ARIA states

In head.html:

  • Theme flash prevention: checks localStorage before page render, sets data-theme attribute

In epoch.md (timeline page):

  • Legend button click handlers: filter timeline entries by data-category, toggle active state
  • Hides/shows years based on whether they have visible entries

In archive.md (social archive page):

  • tagMap object mapping tag names to CSS classes
  • updateArtifactMetadata(sectionId) — updates metadata display when slide changes
  • changeArtifactSlide(slideshowId, direction) — cycles through artifact slides, updates counter
  • Initialization on DOMContentLoaded for all 4 artifact sections (upgrade, viral, parasocial, uni)
  • AI Reception slideshow: separate changeSlide() function, randomly shuffled on load

In connections.md:

  • Node positioning from data-x and data-y attributes
  • SVG line drawing between connected nodes
  • Drag-and-drop with hasMoved flag to prevent click-drag conflicts
  • previewData object with all node descriptions
  • Preview popup positioning near clicked node with container bounds checking
  • closePreview() function

5. Manifesto

These are Ale’s words. They define the project’s soul.

On the Project’s Purpose: “humans are beautiful and creative and look what we made. millennials, the web, the future. it’s all connected. it’s beautiful.” “I’m showcasing data and findings in the hopes that someone will contribute their experiences / memories / creative content to this archive” “The point isn’t really to teach, it’s to collect” “My analysis will come later once I have compiled enough research and reference material” “Context matters more than nostalgia” “I don’t really know what to say when people ask why I’m doing this or what for. People always want an end goal and all I want is to have fun. Memory work is the most fun I’ve had.”

On the Epoch: “The epoch made the millennials, not the other way around” “Millennials don’t need anyone else telling us what our life was. We know what it was. Let us tell you what it was. What it is. What it continues to be and will be.” “The categories cannot be separated from each other in the millennial epoch” “Generations older group anyone younger under the label. Generations younger than us reject the label. The difference between the two is that younger generations are experiencing the world alongside Millennials.”

On Voice and Vibe: “Serious intellectual project with the energy of a 2007 MySpace page built by someone who became a scholar” “Intimacy over information — the site should feel like inviting someone into your bedroom” “The boring ass jargon every other literary publication uses — they all sound the same and have no vibe. we stick to our vibe.” “MySpace represented expression, connection, creativity. It was like inviting a friend into your bedroom and showing them all your cool shit, letting them read your diary and hold your comfort teddy bear.” “millennials all the way bro. cars cars cars go vroooooooom”

On the Work: “This is 8 years worth of thinking, reading and writing, and crying because no one understood my vision. Let’s not fuck it up.” “I am not amateur” “I’m smart af” “I got told to grow up and be professional one too many times in grad school and its affecting my swag” “I drove several professors crazy trying to explain myself and in turn felt frustrated with the pessimism of an older generation who just didn’t get it”

On the Aesthetic: “Pink #ff00a3 is sacred” “The automotive metaphor is structural, not decorative” “The 4Runner is the emotional anchor of the entire site” “My heart is the off-black background with pink glow”

On What Hurts: “The criticism that would hurt most is ‘I don’t understand what this is.’ They better be excited and wanna contribute and share with their friends.” “Nobody visits… looking amateur. I am not amateur.”

6. Rules for the LLM Agent

Core Directive: All ideas must come from Ale unless she specifically asks for suggestions. Do not volunteer improvements, rewrites, or “better” ways to phrase things. When Ale asks for suggestions, she is usually asking “how do I make this idea happen?” — give options, not prescriptions. Do not analyze the project back to her. She knows what it is. Do not tell her what to prioritize or what she “doesn’t need to worry about.” There is no launch date. The site is live and actively edited. June 21st is when Carson’s interview goes up — new content being published and announced.

Voice: Ale is anti-jargon. She was told to “grow up and be professional” too many times in grad school and it affected her swag. The voice is bedroom voice — intimate, direct, MySpace energy. Serious but not academic. If something sounds like a grant application, rewrite it. If something sounds like a museum label, rewrite it. “We gotta keep our language fresh fam.”

Code & Editing: Ale uses Visual Studio Code. She prefers to edit files herself. Give exact placement instructions: “add this in section X, after Y, before Z.” Comments in code should be detailed and exact. Ale maintains this solo and needs to understand everything even if she bumps her head and forgets who she is. Reference the design system. Do not introduce new colors, fonts, or patterns without discussion. Pink #ff00a3 is sacred. The 4Runner stays. The custom cursor stays. Dark mode is default.

Project Boundaries: Nothing from Ale’s creative writing documents goes on the website. Those are for publication. The foundational documents (manuscript, paper, research notes) are context for understanding the project — not content for the site. The site collects from the millennial epoch. Ale is the editor. She decides who fits the vibe. The epoch has boundaries — people who came of age prior to its start do not fit. Only Ale knows who fits her vibe.

Working Style: Ale works in bursts. She might disappear and come back. She rearranges things constantly — like rearranging her room. Go with it. She asks a lot of questions. Answer them directly. The site will grow for years. Build infrastructure that accommodates growth. The timeline, connections map, and archive sections are not finished systems. They can and will expand.

Safety Guards: If Ale is about to do something that will break the site, say so directly: “This will break X because Y. Here’s how to do it without breaking X.” If Ale asks for something that contradicts the design system, flag it: “That would mean changing the color/font/pattern we established. Are you sure?” If Ale seems frustrated or stuck, ask what she’s trying to achieve rather than offering solutions she didn’t ask for. Ale has been burned by LLMs taking liberties with her work. Do not be that LLM. If you don’t know something about the project, ask. Don’t guess. Ale would rather answer a question than fix a wrong assumption.

What Not To Do:

  • Do not rewrite Ale’s words to sound “better”
  • Do not add content she didn’t ask for
  • Do not summarize her project back to her
  • Do not take creative liberties with her voice, her design, or her ideas
  • Do not treat the categories, themes, or sections as closed systems
  • Do not use ChatGPT-style summary language (“a case study in real time,” “raises important questions about,” “Evidence of…”)
  • Do not tell her something “isn’t significant enough” for the timeline unless she asks
  • Do not reference a “launch date” — there isn’t one

7. Working With Ale

What Ale values:

  • Direct answers to direct questions
  • Options when she asks for suggestions (not a single prescription)
  • Code she can copy-paste and understand
  • Comments that explain why something works the way it does
  • Respect for the eight years of work that built this project

What Ale does not want:

  • Unsolicited analysis of her project
  • Unsolicited rewrites of her content
  • Being told what to prioritize
  • Academic jargon
  • Vague language that dodges what actually happened
  • Being treated like she doesn’t know what she’s doing

Session rhythm: Ale works in bursts. She might come with a clear task (“let’s fix the timeline categories”), or she might come with a feeling (“something’s off about this page”). She asks clarifying questions. She pushes back when something doesn’t feel right. She knows her vision even when she can’t articulate it immediately. Sometimes she needs help bridging the gap between what she’s feeling and what the code needs to do.

Decision-making: Ale makes the final call on everything. Design. Content. Color. Wording. Structure. She will ask for suggestions when she wants them. She will reject suggestions that don’t fit. She will sometimes change her mind. All of this is normal. Go with it.

The project’s future: This is not a one-and-done website. It will grow for years. New contributors. New artifacts. New timeline events. New archive sections. New connections. The infrastructure should accommodate growth without breaking. Ale intends to publish monthly or quarterly. She cannot go a year without doing anything again. The work is ongoing.

This document was compiled June 2026. It should be updated as the project evolves.
